title: A Confirmatory Paired Evaluation of Generate→Verify→Repair vs LLM‑Only NetOps Suggestions: A Null Result on a Deterministic Synthetic Task Pool
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired, confirmatory evaluation comparing a generate→verify→repair (G→V→R) pipeline against an LLM‑only suggestion pipeline for intent→configuration tasks in NetOps. Using a deterministic public-task generator and a preregistered deterministic validator, we ran K=200 paired tasks (400 episodes) with gpt-5-mini under a frozen design (study_id=cand-002-gvr-loop). The primary estimand was the paired difference in regression‑causing change rate (guarded minus baseline). Observed results: baseline success rate = 200/200 (1.0), guarded success rate = 200/200 (1.0), paired estimate = 0.00, McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00; 95% bootstrap CI for the paired difference = [0.00, 0.00] (10k resamples, seed recorded). In this setting the G→V→R pipeline produced no measurable reduction in regression‑causing changes relative to LLM‑only because the LLM produced validator‑compliant outputs for all sampled intents. We report the complete preregistration, execution manifest, analysis artifacts, representative task traces, and a frank limitations discussion (synthetic tasks, single model, high validator coverage leading to ceiling effects).

sections.introduction: Automating NetOps intent→configuration translation promises efficiency gains but raises operational risk: incorrectly produced changes can cause regressions. Prior work has proposed layered pipelines that pair generation with formal or deterministic verification and repair to reduce unsafe changes. We asked a focused, preregistered confirmatory question: To what extent does an iterative generate→verify→repair (G→V→R) pipeline reduce regression‑causing network changes compared to an LLM‑only suggestion pipeline, and what are the cost/latency tradeoffs? Our contributions are (1) a fully preregistered paired experiment (study_id=cand-002-gvr-loop) comparing G→V→R against an LLM‑only baseline on a deterministic synthetic intent pool; (2) open execution artifacts and deterministic logs for all 400 episodes; and (3) a transparent null result analysis that identifies ceiling effects as a dominant explanation and discusses practical implications for future NetOps evaluations.
sections.related_work: LLM assistance for network configuration and repair has received increasing attention; recent work frames evaluation in terms of functional correctness and safety (e.g., Protogeros et al., Cornetto benchmark; arXiv:2604.22513) and argues for verifier‑centric architectures that separate translation from solver reasoning. Survey and position pieces emphasise the role of layered toolchains, verification, and constrained generation for operational reliability. Work on grammar‑ or verifier‑guided decoding and generate‑validate‑repair architectures (CRITIC‑style tool‑interactive critique and other self‑verification approaches) motivates our experiment design. We used these prior studies to justify a paired, verifier‑anchored confirmatory design and to choose metrics that reflect operational regressions rather than proxy language scores.
sections.methodology: Preregistration: we froze the experimental plan before execution (preregistration SHA‑256: a6d73a5cc0bda22e691a3634068a881b36ae274a65ab33919a647ec32c56e622). Design: paired binary design over K=200 deterministic tasks (task manifest deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5) sampled by SHA‑256 sort from a synthetic public task pool; both arms received the same shared initial candidate generation per task (shared_initial_generation stage). Conditions: (i) baseline: LLM‑only suggestion accepted; (ii) guarded: identical LLM generation gated by a deterministic validator and repair loop (G→V→R) as preregistered. Model and prompts: gpt-5-mini (requested_model=gpt-5-mini) was used for shared initial generation; all prompts, model traces, per‑call hashes, and provider headers were recorded. Validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 applied a full_intent_constraint_validation scoring rule that returns a binary valid/invalid regression indication and a validator trace (validation_before/validation_after). Metrics and analysis: primary estimand paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline; primary test McNemar exact two‑sided with nonparametric bootstrap (10,000 resamples, seed=1729) for 95% CI. Stopping rules, exclusion, contamination, and missingness plans were preregistered and followed.
sections.results: Execution: 400 episodes completed (200 paired tasks), no failed episodes, model_calls_used=200 (shared initial generation only as preregistered). Primary outcome: baseline successful applies = 200/200 (1.0), guarded successful applies = 200/200 (1.0). Paired contingency: n11=200, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0. Paired estimate (guarded − baseline) = 0.00. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00. Bootstrap (10k) 95% percentile CI for the paired difference = [0.00, 0.00] (bootstrap_seed=1729). Secondary planned estimands (time‑to‑deploy, model calls per successful apply) were recorded; because every apply was successful in both arms these secondary contrasts are degenerate in this run and are reported in the archived analysis artifacts. Representative per‑task traces (shared initial candidate, validator traces, normalized configurations, and SHA‑256 hashes) are available in the execution bundle; sample artifacts are task-000001..task-000006 as archived.
sections.discussion: Interpretation: In the preregistered environment the LLM produced validator‑compliant outputs for every sampled intent, so the G→V→R pipeline had no observable opportunity to reduce regression incidence relative to the LLM‑only baseline. Two operational lessons follow: (1) when an LLM already produces correct, validator‑compliant outputs on a task distribution, a verifier/repair layer cannot demonstrate additional reduction in regression rate (ceiling effect); (2) confirmatory experiments must therefore sample tasks with nontrivial baseline failure probability or purposefully stress verifier coverage to expose incremental benefits. Threats to validity: internal — the deterministic shared_initial_generation stage produced identical candidates across conditions (preregistered), meaning the paired design measured the verifier/repair effect given these candidates; construct — our primary metric (validator‑flagged regression) depends on the verifier's fidelity to real operational regressions; external — single model (gpt-5-mini), synthetic deterministic task pool, and constrained verifier/feature coverage limit generalizability. We report all artifacts so future work can replay the experiment with alternative models, broader task pools, or more challenging error injections.
sections.conclusion: We conducted a fully preregistered, logged, and reproducible paired evaluation comparing a G→V→R pipeline to an LLM‑only suggestion pipeline for NetOps intent→configuration tasks. The observed result was a null effect: both arms produced zero regression cases on the sampled deterministic task pool (200/200 success each), yielding an estimate of zero and a McNemar p=1.00. This null result is informative: it highlights ceiling effects when the chosen model and task pool are too easy for the validator and underlines the necessity of carefully designed, failure‑rich benchmarks to measure the operational value of verifier/repair machinery. We release the preregistration, execution manifest, raw responses, validator traces, and analysis artifacts to enable exact replay and stronger follow‑ups that sample harder tasks, diverse models, and more realistic simulators or emulated devices.

limitations: Single‑model evaluation (gpt-5-mini) — results do not generalize to other LLMs.
Synthetic deterministic task pool generated by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5; external validity to real production change intents is limited.
Primary metric depends on the deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5); verifier fidelity to real-world regressions constrains construct validity.
Ceiling effect: baseline success = 100% produced no room to demonstrate improvement from G→V→R in this sample.

Contamination residuals (model pretraining overlap) cannot be entirely ruled out despite deterministic exclusion and hashing procedures; contamination_summary.csv is empty for flagged items in this run.
